doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Race, hiring and the common ground of musicians
summary: Nussbaum says he does not worry about race, notes some people will not hire a white drummer, and says musicians listen rather than look.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What about the racial scene these days? Is it, I mean this music has brought a lot of people together where they weren’t allowed in other parts of society. Is it healthy now for you guys anyway?

You know I’ve never really thought about this stuff in regard to what I do. I just do what I do. I can only try to be the best that I can be. I’m going to be — sorry about that — I know I’m going to be involved in situations and I can only try to play the best I can. I know I won’t get hired by certain white musicians. I know I won’t get hired by certain black musicians. But you know what? Then I know I get hired by certain white musicians and I know I get hired by black musicians. And I’ve found that it’s a strange reality but being a white jazz drummer, there’s not many of me. There’s not many. You know what I’m saying? And I mean there are certain white guys that won’t hire me because I’m white. There’s certain white people within the business that won’t hire me because I’m white. And you know I find that the best musicians that I know, black or white, they don’t look at you, they listen to you. But I don’t let this bother me because I can just go straight ahead and play. So that’s BS for other people to worry about, not me. I just have to go ahead and play my ass off and do the best that I can do. But I understand the reality of it. And I don’t let it faze me. You know people like Art Pepper and all these guys that wrote these books, they were always dealing with that paranoia, you know, oh will I be accepted in this game as this, because I’m going to feel like an outsider. Man, I’m in here with what I’m doing. I don’t worry about that. You know he was always dealing with that and that kind of paranoia and then — I can’t worry about those kind of things. I have friends, black, white, green, you know we’re all the same here, we’re all the same in this world. If people could start looking at how similar we all are instead of how different we are, you know we’re all the same man, we can all get together, black men, white women, white men, black women, yellow people. It makes no difference. We’re all people. We can all get together. It’s not like humans and dogs, you know what I mean? We’re all people in this world. Right? I mean if they could all look at it that way, if we could look at things that way there’d be no more problems happening in Europe with the whole thing

with Yugoslavia and Serbia and this and Croatia and all the Middle Eastern crap. You know I just look at the common — what do we all have in common. Not what do we all have in difference. I don’t know, what would you say about all that?
Oh yeah, and you know there’s nothing in there to argue with. I’m not going to argue with you anyway.
But I mean I don’t worry about this stuff man.

Yeah that’s something that you can’t, you know, it’s like if someone is — really it’s kind of like going back talking about corporate marketing. If somebody is so hung up on this preconceived idea rather than just looking or listening rather at the way someone plays and says yeah I’d like to work with him, I’d like to have him in my band or I hear the way he plays and I don’t want to have him in my band, that’s what it should all be about. And if someone doesn’t happen to think or hear that way then I don’t think I would want to work with them anyway. I wouldn’t really want to be a part of that musical situation. So I never think about it, it all just seems to work out in a natural way.
